subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage:
In the Monday review at the design studio, Pradeep put up his hand before anyone spoke. "The measurements on slide six are mine and they're wrong. Nobody asked, but I couldn't let it go out." He looked tired, not embarrassed. Swati felt her ears burn. Last week she had spotted the same error in her own file and fixed it at midnight, telling no one, because her first thought had been how the team would talk. Their manager said, "Thank you, though next time tell me before the meeting."
At the tea machine Swati said, "You didn't seem to care what people would think." Pradeep laughed. "I cared. I just cared more about sleeping tonight." She thought of the colleagues who might have copied her old figure.

qa.q: On which slide were Pradeep's measurements wrong?
qa.a: The measurements on slide six were wrong.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when Pradeep admitted the error?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, because she had quietly fixed the same kind of error and told nobody.

qa.q: What could Swati try that keeps her care for the team's view but adds what Pradeep showed?
qa.a: She could tell the team or the manager about her own catch, so others can check their figures, while still thinking about how it is said.

qa.q: What does the manager's remark suggest about Pradeep's way of speaking up?
qa.a: The manager thanked Pradeep but asked to be told beforehand, which suggests that speaking up openly without warning has a cost even when honest.

grounding: A person raised with shame norms sees another person at the studio driven by conscience, and each approach shows strengths and blind spots.

passage:
Dear Pankaj,

You asked how the new job is. Odd and interesting. Two colleagues have taught me something without meaning to. Leila will not submit a report until she is sure nobody could find fault. I recognise that; it comes from me too. Tomas, on the other hand, told our manager about his own slip when no one would ever have known, and went home lighter.
I grew up counting who was watching. Tomas seems to count what he can live with. Neither is perfect: Leila's polish sometimes keeps the whole team waiting, and Tomas can confess before he has checked whether the fix is ready. I am trying to borrow a little from each, to think of the people around me and of my own conscience too.
Write soon.

Swati

qa.q: Which colleague told the manager about a slip when no one would have known?
qa.a: Tomas told the manager about a slip when no one would ever have known.

qa.q: What does Swati feel when recognising Leila's habit?
qa.a: Swati feels a mixed, rueful kinship, because the wish to avoid any fault, watched by others, comes from Swati too.

qa.q: What is Swati trying to do after seeing both colleagues?
qa.a: Swati is trying to borrow a little from each: keep thinking of the people around and also listen to conscience, to avoid the weakness each shows.

qa.q: What are the drawbacks of Leila's approach, as seen by the team?
qa.a: Leila's polish sometimes keeps the whole team waiting, because the report is not submitted until nobody could find fault.

grounding: A person raised with shame norms observes colleagues who fear their own conscience, and sees strengths and blind spots in each.
